title: The Great Cedar Cut Down: A Warning to Pharaoh
summary: Ezekiel asks Pharaoh whom he resembles in greatness and answers with a parable of a towering cedar, Assyria, watered by the deep and envied by every tree in Eden. Because it grew proud of its height, God handed it over to a ruthless conqueror, cut it down, and sent it to Sheol. Egypt, the oracle concludes, will follow it into the depths of the earth.
story: Chapter 31 belongs to the block of oracles against Egypt (chapters 29 to 32), the largest group in Ezekiel's words against the nations. Judah's last kings had pinned their hopes on Egypt as a counterweight to Babylon, and Zedekiah's rebellion depended on that help. The previous chapter ended with God breaking Pharaoh's arm; this one asks Egypt to look at history. The empire that had dominated the Near East for generations had just collapsed, and Egypt was no taller. The chapter moves the book toward its turning point in chapter 33, when news of Jerusalem's fall arrives, by stripping away the last human refuge the exiles might have trusted.
historical:
The oracle is dated to the first day of the third month of the eleventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, around June 587 BC, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. Egypt's Pharaoh was Hophra (called Apries by Greek writers), who had sent an army that briefly drew the Babylonians away from the city (Jeremiah 37:5-11). The hope that Egypt could save Judah was real, and Ezekiel attacks it directly.

The comparison with Assyria was fresh. Assyria had been the great power of the Near East for much of the previous three centuries, the empire that destroyed Samaria in 722 BC. Yet its capital Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, and the last Assyrian resistance was crushed within a few years. The ruler of the nations in verse 11 is best taken as Nebuchadnezzar or Babylon, the same hand now raised against Egypt. A small textual note: some scholars suggest that the word for Assyria in verse 3 should be read as the name of a kind of tree, making the whole parable about Egypt alone. Most translations, including the BSB, keep Assyria, and the chapter reads naturally as a lesson drawn from Assyria's fall.
cultural:
The cedars of Lebanon were the prize timber of the ancient world. Kings of Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon sent expeditions to cut them, and Solomon built the temple with them. A cedar was therefore a natural figure for royal majesty, and Mesopotamian and Israelite writers alike used the image of a world tree whose shade shelters all creatures. Daniel 4 gives Nebuchadnezzar a dream about exactly such a tree. Ezekiel had already used cedar imagery for the house of David in chapter 17.

The tree here is rooted in the deep (the Hebrew tehom, the waters beneath the earth), and it grows in the garden of God, Eden. Egypt's whole life depended on the Nile, so a tree fed by abundant waters fitted it well. Sheol was the Israelite name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a pit beneath the earth. To lie among the uncircumcised was a particular shame for Egyptians, who practiced circumcision; Ezekiel threatens them with a burial among those they despised.
literary: The chapter is an extended parable in three movements, framed by a question to Pharaoh at the start and the same question at the end. Verses 2 to 9 describe the tree's glory with lavish repetition: its height, its branches, its waters, its shade. Verses 10 to 14 give the verdict, introduced by the prophetic formula, with its reason: the tree grew proud. Verses 15 to 18 follow the tree down to Sheol and describe the mourning of creation and the strange comfort of the other fallen trees below. The closing line, "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude", turns the parable on its hearer the way Nathan's words did on David.

outline.t: Date and question: whom is Pharaoh like?
The cedar of Assyria in its glory
Cut down for its pride, a warning to all trees
The descent to Sheol and the mourning of creation

doctrines.note: God claims both the tree's rise and its fall: "I made it beautiful with its many branches" (verse 9), and "I delivered it into the hand of the ruler of the nations" (verse 11). Empires are not self-made, and they do not outlast the one who gave them their height.

The stated reason for Assyria's fall is pride: "it grew proud on account of its height" (verse 10). Judgment on nations in Ezekiel is not random; it answers self-exaltation, and it is meant as a warning to others (verse 14).

Every tree, however tall, is "consigned to death" and goes down "among the mortals who descend to the Pit" (verse 14). The chapter levels the great with the ordinary: kings and empires share human mortality.

words.note: Erez, cedar. The great tree of Lebanon, prized for building palaces and temples. The word carries associations of royalty and permanence, which is why its felling is so striking.

Gobah, height. Used here both for the tree's literal height and, through the related verb in verse 10, for pride. In Hebrew, being high and being haughty are close together, and the chapter plays on that link.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. In most of the Old Testament it is the shadowy place where all the dead go, not a place of torment in particular. Here it is the destination of the proud tree and its allies, the end of all worldly greatness.
Arel, uncircumcised. For Israel and for Egypt alike, lying among the uncircumcised meant dishonor in death. The word prepares for the long lament over Egypt's descent in chapter 32.

christ: The link here is thematic rather than predictive. The Bible repeatedly pictures great kingdoms as trees that shelter the nations and are cut down for their pride (Ezekiel 17 and 31, Daniel 4). Against that background, Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, that grows into a tree in whose branches the birds of the air nest (Matthew 13:31-32; Mark 4:30-32). The image of the sheltering tree returns, but its greatness begins in smallness and comes from God. The chapter's lesson, that God brings down the proud, is also sung by Mary (Luke 1:52), and it is fulfilled most deeply in the one who humbled himself and was exalted by God (Philippians 2:5-11).

hard.q: Egypt was not destroyed like Assyria. Did this prophecy fail?
hard.a: Egypt did survive as a nation, and the prophecy should be read on its own terms. The chapter is a poetic warning about Pharaoh's pride and power, cast in the language of a felled tree and a descent to Sheol. Babylon did defeat Egypt's ambitions in Asia, Nebuchadnezzar campaigned against Egypt in the 560s BC (a Babylonian text records a campaign in his thirty-seventh year, around 568 BC), and Egypt never again became the great power it had been, falling later to Persia. Some readers see this as the substance of fulfillment. Others note that prophetic oracles against the nations use conventional, sweeping imagery and that Ezekiel himself later revised an expectation about Tyre (29:17-20), which suggests the prophets did not treat such oracles as fixed timetables. Either way, the point the chapter presses, that Egypt was no safe refuge, proved true.

questions: The tree's height and beauty were gifts from God (verse 9), yet they became the occasion of its pride. Where do good gifts in your life tempt you toward self-sufficiency?
Judah looked to Egypt for rescue from Babylon. What powers or institutions do people trust in the way Judah trusted Egypt?
The fall of Assyria was meant to warn every other tree (verse 14). What does it take for someone to learn from another's downfall rather than repeat it?
